title: Judge tosses Trump's attempt to block Alaska Senate results if GOP incumbent loses
description: President Trump listens as Republican Se
body:
President Trump listens as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who is running for reelection, speaks at an Oct. 13 campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska.
                
                    Alex Brandon/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Brandon/AP
    

   
   A federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's highly unusual attempt to block the certification of results from a key U.S. Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent loses.   In a ruling released Sunday, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason found the federal government does not have the ability to bring this lawsuit, which cited the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act.   It asked the judge to stop state officials from certifying election results to allow for an investigation into whether voters were confused by having two similarly named Senate candidates appear on Alaska's ranked-choice ballot.   
   But Judge Gleason concluded that such a court order would likely violate Alaskan voters' right to a secret ballot.   "The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling," wrote Gleason, a nominee of former President Barack Obama.   The Justice Department is planning to appeal, spokesperson Kiersten Pels told NPR in a statement. "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," Pels added.   
   Voting rights groups that stepped in to help defend Alaska against the lawsuit cheered the ruling.   "DOJ's attempt to throw out Alaska's election results before a single ballot was counted was lawless from the start, and the court saw it for exactly what it was. It was a reckless waste of taxpayer money aimed at silencing hundreds of thousands of Alaska voters," Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Voting Rights Project, said in a statement.   President Trump said he ordered this lawsuit to be filed because out of the four Senate candidates on Alaska's ballot, two have similar names — Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, and Daniel Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with a political party.   
   Alaska's Republican Party supported an earlier effort in state court that tried to keep Sullivan Jr., the non-incumbent, off the ballot. But in June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled Sullivan Jr. has the right to run as a candidate.   Still, Republican allegations of Democrats propping up Sullivan Jr. to spoil the incumbent Sullivan's chances of winning reelection have long hung over this closely watched Senate contest.   A New York Times report about Democratic campaign operatives' efforts to recruit Sullivan Jr. — which NPR has not independently confirmed — drew new attention to those allegations. Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation and indicated the results of the race may not be certified by the state depending on how that investigation turns out.   "If we find out there's wrongdoing, and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that's what happens," Dunleavy said during an Oct. 30 interview with NewsNation.   At an Oct. 30 press conference in Anchorage, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman said there is an "ongoing" criminal probe by the Justice Department.   The Democratic candidate, former Rep. Mary Peltola, has denied any involvement.   In an interview Sunday with CNN's State of the Union, incumbent Sullivan said that he would accept the election results, win or lose.   This controversy hasn't stopped Alaskans from voting. Over 86,700 voters in the state have cast their ballots during early voting, according to the latest figures from Alaska's Division of Elections. And more Alaskans are expected to exercise their rights as voting continues through Tuesday's Election Day.   Additional reporting by NPR's Eric McDaniel. Edited by Benjamin Swasey

title: Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy is hospitalized with a stroke
description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., appears at a
body:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., appears at a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on September 18, 2025. Murphy's office says he was hospitalized this weekend with a stroke.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
    

   
   Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., has been hospitalized following a stroke, according to his office.   In a statement on Sunday, Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said he is expected to make a full recovery.   "Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game," Herwitt wrote. "He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment."   Murphy, 53, is a prominent figure in the party and has been a prolific campaign surrogate for candidates through the midterm cycle. Viewed as a possible 2028 presidential contender, Murphy has carved out a position as a foreign policy leader and champion of aggressive executive branch oversight.   
   He recently returned from a multistop tour in the Middle East, after which he warned that President Trump would dramatically escalate his war on Iran after the midterm election.   The lawmaker is the latest in a string of lawmakers to experience a health crisis this year. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., missed months of Senate work during a lengthy hospital stay and rehabilitation process. Rep. Tom Kean, R-N.J., was missing from the Capitol for months for what he later announced was treatment for depression.   In 2022, three prominent Democratic lawmakers — Sen. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico, Chis Van Hollen of Maryland, and then-Senate candidate John Fetterman — were all hospitalized for strokes.

title: The midterms will test the nation's political direction and confidence
description: Voting stickers rest at Contra Costa Cou
body:
Voting stickers rest at Contra Costa County's election operations facility on May 27, 2026 in Martinez, Calif.
                
                    Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images
    

   
   Millions of Americans are looking to Tuesday's midterm elections with heightened anticipation or anxiety.   Or both.   At this point, we can expect at least some portion of the nation to have its political confidence — and perhaps even its sense of security — tested in the days and weeks ahead. That test could also continue for some time to come.   Is winter coming for MAGA?   The first place to look for elevated anxiety about the midterms would be among those voters most loyal to President Trump. He calls them MAGA, borrowing from his 2016 "Make America Great Again" theme. Alternatively, with a broad smile, he just calls them "my base."   
   But winter may be coming. Polling suggests that on Tuesday the midterm electoral pendulum will once again swing back against the White House incumbent — as it has in every midterm over the last 100 years with very few exceptions.   More punishment for the party of the second-term president would be expected in the blue states that he lost in each of his three White House campaigns. But this fall's polls are also pointing to significant losses for Republicans in swing states and even in some of the red states Trump won all three times — often by double-digit margins.   That is why the president spent the last weekend of this campaign on making an electoral "goal line stand" for the Senate by visiting Iowa and Kansas.   When Trump, then a first-time candidate, was at high tide 10 years ago, he won 31 Iowa counties that had previously voted for Democrat Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012. And as for Kansas, the historically Republican state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.   Yet Trump put live visits to Iowa and Kansas on his schedule for the final weekend, even as he did remote "tele-rallies" in 19 other states. (The Iowa-Kansas plan was briefly cancelled late in the pre-election week, then reinstated just before the weekend.)   
   That strategy suggests Trump's political team remains focused on limiting GOP losses in what will be a tough environment for their party. Most observers, including those searching hardest for objective measurements, now predict Trump's party will lose its slim majority in the House. The consensus is that the Senate is too close to call, and it is possible the GOP could hold the majority using the tie-breaking vote to which Vice President Vance is entitled.   Best way to limit losses?   
   But precedent is not really the explanation for Trump and his party's expected defeats. Midterm elections inevitably act as referenda on current officeholders, and there is no current officeholder in the world so visible as the U.S. president — especially the Oval Office's current mega-mediagenic occupant. Put another way, presidents are the leaders and symbols of their party, but Trump has taken the personalization to another level. Presidents routinely campaign for their party's midterm candidates, but Trump ("Pretend I'm on the ballot") has worked hard to make the election about himself.   In Trump's first term he tried out a more conventional approach, acting as an executive in a system of shared powers. This time around, Trump has taken that role as a starting point. He has cast himself as the driver of historic events and the avenger of many wrongs — large or small, real or imagined. He presents himself as the architect of a new Washington and the author of a new era.   And he has done it all despite objections from U.S. allies around the world and from Congress and from the federal bench.   How it's playing depends on audience   While Trump's bravura interpretation of his role has played well with his base, the larger electorate is a different story. Among the more effective themes taken up by anti-Trump rallies has been the ultra-simple, anti-autocrat mantra of "No Kings."   
   Critics and Democrats have been able to focus on promises and pronouncements Trump has made but on which he has yet to deliver. Peace in Ukraine on Day 1? A new era for Israel and the Palestinians? Not so far.   
   These foreign policy issues matter, but to voters the greater disappointment is economic. Trump said he would make things cheaper and tame inflation. But inflation remains elevated and the public sees the price of gas leading a sustained surge in everyday costs.   So it should be no surprise that any average of Trump's recent approval numbers shows them falling from a clear majority (52% in average of polls) early in 2025 to an average of 37% now — breaking below the 40% threshold that has signaled brutal midterm results in the past.   But are Democrats ready to take over?   On the other hand, the confidence some Democrats are showing may be premature. If they win the House, their majority will be on the modest side by historic standards. If they eke out a majority in the Senate it will be so narrow that the primary beneficiaries are likely to be the mavericks who are willing to buck the party leadership — on both sides of the aisle.   Moreover, even robust Democratic majorities would need to confront the significant divisions that persist — and may be growing — in their ranks. The most glaring is the contrast between majoritarian consensus builders on one hand and the party's firebrands on the left. The latter group has been pleased with the party's class of nominees for Congress this year, including a cadre aligned or associated with the Democratic Socialists of America.   The DSA candidates have attracted attention from the media and been prominently featured in Republicans' fall campaign ads and messaging, even in places where the DSA favorite lost in the primary and is not on the November ballot.   
   To some degree, the 2026 Democrats have been able to unite around issues such as energy and grocery prices and the war on Iran. Opposing vast data centers to be built to serve the AI industry has been another shared cause. And whatever their differences, this year's Democrats have been a chorus of opposition to Trump.   But there are reasons to doubt the united front can be preserved if the Democrats get back into power. Most expect at least one chamber of Congress to be theirs in the new year, and there will be a new president after 2028.   
   One political demographer and author who has been focused on the Democrats' internal issues is Ruy Teixeira, who spent most of his career at think tanks associated with Democrats such as the Center for American Progress and the Brookings Institution but is now at the business-oriented American Enterprise Institute. He is best known for his 2002 book with John Judis entitled, The Emerging Democratic Majority, but Teixeira has long been focused on the party's history with white, non-college educated voters and is also the author with Joel Rogers of America's Forgotten Majority: Why The White Working Class Still Matters.   In October, Teixeira published 11 questions he said Democrats must confront if they regain congressional power. The final question was whether the party would embrace positions that resonate with working-class voters and prioritize their interests rather than its recent concentration on race, gender, energy, environment and social policy.   Casting a longer shadow    Beyond the questions for the two major parties, these midterms have cast doubt on the conduct of U.S. elections themselves. For generations, Americans have generally shown confidence in their electoral systems and results, but that too has become a target.   There is a haunting song on Eric Clapton's classic 1992 album Unplugged that repeats the title line: "Running on Faith."   
   That is one way to think of democracy. Faith in the democratic system is required if the system is going to work and survive.   Democracy has often been called an ongoing experiment. It tests whether people can have a voice in their own governing, and whether that voice can be heard and heeded.   It tests the mechanisms and individuals involved, to be sure. But ultimately, it tests voters' faith in the system itself. Will the will of the people be clear and will it drive the next phase of American political life?   Nonpartisan experts in voting laws and machinery — academics, journalists, lawyers and others — have, as a rule, defended the current state of American processes. Legislation, administrative professionalism and fresh funding at the national and state levels have upgraded the administration of American elections since the Help America Vote Act became law two decades ago, following the Florida vote-counting debacle in the year 2000. HAVA enabled states and localities to replace punch-card ballots and other outdated methods with touch-screen technology and preservable paper trails, improving voter confidence and security.   And yet, faith in the system is likely to be tested in the days ahead. It's not just about one race or one state. It's not just about candidates and issues. It's about the system that Trump repeatedly calls into question without evidence.   A well-established pattern   As far back as his first nomination in 2016, Trump was telling his crowds that if he lost it would be because the process was fraudulent. There was no way the Democrats could win unless they cheated, he said, and a defeat would simply prove his assertion.   Four years later, Trump was able to summon thousands of his supporters to Washington on Jan. 6, 2021 to protest and deny his defeat in the previous November's presidential election. "Stop the steal" was the cry, based on nothing but conjecture and emotion and a preference for a different outcome.   
   In contrast, Trump accepted the results in 2024 as he and his party won. But he continues to label information — be it polling results or simple daily news reporting — as fake. He responds to a question from a White House credentialed reporter by asking: "Who are you with?" Then he says: "You're fake news."   He regularly tells his audiences to ignore "fake news" and "fake polls." It is easy to imagine him exhorting his followers to ignore "fake results."   There will be tension on election night this week, as there always is. But the greater stress may come in the days and weeks ahead.   Stay tuned.

schema.headline: The midterms will test the nation's political direction and confidence

title: How to think about the midterms — and the political moment the country is in
description: President Donald Trump spoke to members
body:
President Donald Trump spoke to members of the media during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club on October 31, 2026 in Palm Beach, Florida.
                
                    Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America
    

   
   📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App      President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices. But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, record-high intensity of opposition, and voters are blaming him for prices that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around.   Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy. But the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased prices on goods and energy.   
   The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well, in large part, because of increasing stock portfolios dominated by AI companies, while regular Americans are turning against AI data centers, struggling because of inflation that is outpacing wages, a middling labor market and interest rates that are creeping higher. Those rates are making it harder to buy a home or a car, making millions of people feel like they're treading water.   The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll showed a plurality — 44% — said their finances have mostly stayed the same and another 38% saying their economic situations have worsened. Only 15% said things have actually gotten better for them from a money standpoint.   Add to that the disapproval of the administration's hard-line immigration enforcement tactics, cuts to domestic spending on programs like Medicaid and other health care programs, and the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's angering swing voters and firing up Democrats.   As a result, the president's party is likely to pay the price. Midterms are usually difficult for the president's party to begin with.   History is not on Republicans' side this year    Only twice since World War II has the president's party gained seats in the House in a midterm election. On average, the president's party loses 26 seats in midterm years, and it's worse when a president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's has been. When that's the case, the presidents' parties have lost an average of 35 seats. When they're above 50%, they still lose seats but only 15 on average, 20 seats better than when a president is unpopular.   
   The fact that presidents' parties lose seats in midterms is something Trump himself has acknowledged multiple times at campaign events.   Meanwhile, Democrats have had political success in this Trump term. They have consistently overperformed in special elections, which are indicators of midterm prowess, and they cleaned up in the 2025 off-year elections. Since then, the political landscape has only gotten worse for Republicans because of the unpopular Iran war that has led to skyrocketing gas prices.   All of that points to Democratic gains this cycle. They are favored to win control of the House, and they are in striking distance of winning the Senate, something that had been seen as a longshot at the beginning of this cycle.   Democrats have potential limitations   While the landscape has undoubtedly moved more in Democrats' direction over the last several months, the extent of the likely potential gains is not clear.   A big reason for that is structural. When looking at the Cook Political Report's ratings, there are about 30 fewer competitive districts — ones rated as lean or toss up — this year than in 2018 when Democrats won a net gain of more than 40 seats in the House.   Mid-decade redistricting has also helped to insulate Republicans this cycle, even if marginally. After all the redistricting fights across the country, with Trump explicitly pushing GOP-led state legislatures to get more Republican seats, an NPR analysis shows Republicans netted an estimated 8-seat advantage out of redistricting.   Depending on how Latinos in South Texas, in particular, vote those gains might be lower.   
   While Republicans face significant headwinds and the GOP is not viewers favorably, the Democratic Party is also not viewed positively. Democrats have had trouble wrangling a base of voters who should be Democrats but are restive and unsatisfied by the party.   That said, the latest NPR poll showed that self-identified "democratic socialists" were very engaged in these midterms and hotly disapprove of the job Trump is doing.   As the old saying goes, the enemy of my enemy is my friend. This group of voters may vote in big numbers in this election as a check on Trump — 44% of poll respondents said their vote was a vote against Trump while 21% said it was a vote for him. But there's a likely clash of ideals and approach coming on the left over the next several months, as the Democratic presidential primaries.   
   And make no mistake, the 2028 election begins almost immediately after these midterms. It's an open election — the first one post-Trump, post-Obama-Biden, post-Clintons and Bushes. Candidates who want to make a splash and need a national boost tend to announce earlier rather than later. Think: January, February.   
   It's important to remember nothing is a done deal until the results are in. A lot of this is going to come down to Republican turnout.   That's why Trump has been deployed to red states to try and push and plead with his base to get out and vote. Without a big GOP turnout in these places, a one- or two-seat pick up for Democrats in the Senate can quickly turn into six or seven.   Be ready for surprises. But if Democrats don't win the House, it would be the shocker of all shockers and represent a polling error like we haven't seen this century.   Prepare to be patient   While most states and districts will be called by the time people go to bed on election night, some will not. Those lingering races may be in key places, and given the margins, particularly in the Senate, it's possible party control won't be known for days, if not weeks.   Trump is already laying the groundwork for claims of rigged elections. That's no surprise. He's done that after every election that hasn't gone his way previously in one way or another. After the 2020 election, his false claims of fraud led to the Jan. 6 siege at the Capitol.   
   The latest NPR poll found most people across parties overwhelmingly believe their states will run fair and accurate elections and that their preferred candidate should accept the outcome, no matter what it is.   But a quarter of Republicans said their candidate likely shouldn't accept the results. That leaves room for potential chaos and misinformation if elections are close and not decided for weeks.   Trump has been a clear drag on the GOP this cycle. You don't have to believe polls to know it's the case. Look at what Republican candidates are doing. Their mentions in ads of Trump during the primaries were sky high.   
   Now, they're nearly nonexistent.   Republicans will admit privately that Trump is a double-edged sword — he's needed with the base, but toxic with swing voters.   And that's been the story of Trump for the past decade — beloved by an ardent slice of the country and loathed by an even bigger one.   But this year, with the economic strain on people and the U.S.'s continued involvement in the kind of ongoing war he promised to keep the country out of, polls have found consistently over a long period of time this year that his support with many of those who crossed over to vote for him in 2024 has cratered.   That hardly sets up Trump and his party for success Tuesday and beyond — despite what will be claims of nefariousness that will hold little weight. But that doesn't mean either party will have massive majorities, and compromise will be necessary to get big things done.

schema.headline: How to think about the midterms — and the political moment the country is in

title: Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate in Michigan Senate race, spurning Abdul El-Sayed
body:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right, and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., attend a service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit.
                
                    Jose Juarez/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jose Juarez/AP
    

   
   DETROIT — After months of proclaiming support for the Democratic ticket, Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her former primary rival Abdul El-Sayed, less than 48 hours before Election Day.   "As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video she posted to social media on Sunday. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the U.S. Senate today."   Her statement followed a surprise appearance with Rogers at a church in Detroit.   
   Outside a "Souls to the Polls" event at a church in Detroit, El-Sayed told reporters that he doesn't think about Stevens and said voters do not either.   "None of this matters," El-Sayed said. "You know what matters. You can go, like, 15 minutes that way, or 15 minutes that way, or 15 minutes that way. And there are families who are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters before a Souls to the Polls campaign event at Northend Church of God in Christ, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit.
                
                    Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
    

   
   In her endorsement, Stevens said she does "not stand with Hasan Piker," a streamer that El-Sayed campaigned with during the primary. In August, after Piker implied that Jews' support for Israel puts them at risk of personal violence, El-Sayed sought to distance himself from the controversy, saying Piker did not speak for the campaign. He stopped short of disavowing Piker.   Stevens had been critical that El-Sayed was not doing enough to reassure Jewish and Black voters who supported her during the primary. Even though relations between the pair had been publicly disintegrating for weeks, Stevens' announcement was a surprise.   
   Tensions accelerated after Stevens' fiance, Jason Turkish, said he planned to vote for Rogers. In a subsequent TV appearance, Stevens maintained she was still planning to support the Democratic nominee. She urged El-Sayed to denounce a recent ad by Cenk Uygur, of Young Turks, that blamed Israel for high grocery prices in the United States.   "The ad tells Michigan families they cannot afford groceries because their money has to be set aside 'for killing Palestinians,' and it blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford," she wrote.   El-Sayed's campaign had said he had nothing to do with the ad and criticized the contents of the ad on Saturday.   Stevens said she was originally scheduled to attend a different church event in Detroit on Sunday alongside El-Sayed and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C. The planned joint appearance was meant to be a unifying event for the party ahead of the election. But on Friday, Stevens set a condition for her participation in the event — that El-Sayed reject the ad and apologize for rhetoric she considered to be inflammatory and offensive.   The event with El-Sayed and Clyburn went ahead as planned, without Stevens.   Stevens' announcement has sent shockwaves through the Democratic Party.   Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it a "despicable betrayal."   "Haley Stevens' decision to campaign with Rogers — a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan's working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump's agenda — shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about," Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said in a statement.   Stevens' communications director has an email auto reply that says as of Sunday, he is no longer working for the Stevens office. On social media, several former campaign staffers slammed their former boss' actions.   
   The clash between the two Michigan Democrats highlights a broader rift within the party as it relates to Israel and rhetoric around Israel. That schism is likely to extend far beyond Election Day and will be something the Democratic Party has to contend with, particularly as it prepares for the 2028 presidential nominating process.

title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., speaks to re
body:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., speaks to reporters in March 2026, in Washington. Murphy suffered a stroke on Saturday and is expected to recover.
                
                    Allison Robbert/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Allison Robbert/AP
    

   
   Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.       The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.   
   Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."    Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.   Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:   
   B – BALANCE loss   Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.   E – EYE changes   Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.   F – FACE drooping   Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.   A – ARM weakness   Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?   S – SPEECH difficulty   Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?   T – TIME to call 911   If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.   A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.   
   Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.   Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

title: It's ACA open enrollment time. Here are the changes for health insurance shoppers
description: Christine Meehan, a hair stylist in Uppe
body:
Christine Meehan, a hair stylist in Upper Chichester, Pa., has purchased health insurance through Pennie, the ACA marketplace for Pennsylvania. She's pictured here in October 2025. ACA open enrollment runs from Nov. 1 through Jan. 15 in most states.
                
                    Tassanee Vejpongsa/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tassanee Vejpongsa/AP
    

   
   Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.   Shoppers need to plan accordingly.   Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts started earlier, and some states have been allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.   A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.   
   But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.   Have your ID ready   One of the biggest changes for people shopping for their 2027 coverage will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents. The requirements are aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.      The new rules, outlined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.   For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.   
   Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed "high-risk" must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as "high-risk" first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.   Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because "someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer."   The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.   The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned "that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing" and may just give up and not get insured.   Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian's help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver's license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.   "Some people may have trouble not because they're not real, but because they don't have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names," said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.   
   She said the changes might "be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles."   There may be fewer brokers   CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.   CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of "significant compliance concerns" in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out "hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers" this year.   
   Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients' coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.   "Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense," he said. However, in the short term, "I don't know if they care about the chaos it will cause."   That's because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he's unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.   He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.   "They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long," Fine said.   
   Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit on Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.   "Just because you're a new agent doesn't mean you are fraudulent," said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. "All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won't be able to work."   It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown's Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. "If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early."   Costs will continue to be an issue   This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.   Still, most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.   The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.   This helps offset premium increases.   "For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same," said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst forHealthInsurance.org. "That's not to say it's great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that."   
   But there are other factors at work, too.   Last year'saverage premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers' fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs and general inflation, and labor shortages.   For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.   Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.   "The biggest issue we will face is affordability," said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. "There definitely will come a breaking point for people."   Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.   "If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity," Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.   That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.   
   The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.   Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.   KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

title: Living with high prices in Virginia's 1st Congressional District
description: A mural off Tappahannock's main road, in
body:
A mural off Tappahannock's main road, in the courtyard next to the Java Jacks Cafe
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A display of t-shirts at Java Jacks Cafe in Tappahannock, Virginia
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   At Java Jacks in the riverside town of Tappahannock, Va., the sausage is savory, the beignet-like jacks are sugar-dusted and you have your choice of t-shirts. You can get a brightly-colored one with an image of the cafe and its slogan, "Come in, We're Awesome," or you can go for something darkly funny that says "Coffee Makes Me Feel Less Murdery."    "We started by selling just the t-shirts of the building. And then we'd gotten a couple of the sarcastic shirts for the staff and the customers were trying to buy them off of our backs," owner Jeans Owens laughs from behind the coffee bar.  Java Jacks started in 2006, in what was once someone's little one-story home on the main road through town. The atmosphere is cozy and friendly, with pictures of smiling customers and staff taped to door frames and to the wall.    
   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Snapshots of happy staff and customers decorate the walls and doors of Java Jacks
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   Owens and her husband took over the business about eight years ago. "What we were interested in was being our own bosses," she says, "and something that could set us up a little better for retirement."   But their first years running the cafe have included the pandemic and inflation: lots of expensive bumps for small business owners.   "Our coffee prices went sky high," she says. They're up over 30% since 2022. The cost of beef is up, so is the cost of sausage and paper products for takeout orders: "To-go boxes. You know there was a time we were paying 12 cents for those," Owens says. Now, it's nearly 30 cents. And to-go cups? "The cup, the lid, the straw used to cost us all together maybe 3 cents." She says it's now more than 20 cents.   The cafe's electricity bill has also recently jumped. "Normally, I'm paying $450, $500 a month," she says. "I'm paying over $1000 now."   Owens says Java Jacks has a loyal customer base and she's been committed to doing whatever she can to keep menu prices affordable, including keeping some meals at $10. She says she now goes to Walmart early in the morning to get milk and juice rather than purchase them from a supplier.  She goes to a local grocery store for fresh fruit. She also regularly checks prices between three suppliers and switches between them, depending on which one has the lowest costs.   It's not just Owens' habits that have changed, it's her customers': she's noticed more senior citizens sharing orders. "We had like maybe one or two when we bought [Java Jacks], but now we'll have multiple tickets a day that are split." Some customers are adjusting how they tip her staff, too. "They tend to be tipped very well just because we're a small atmosphere," Owens says. But when the price of gas shot up, the tips got smaller. "When [gas] came back down, we started seeing that trend change," she says.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                From behind the coffee bar, cafe owner Jeans Owens shows NPR's Ayesha Rascoe the Java Jacks menu
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   Owens feels she's handling the increase in costs as best she can, though she is having to increase menu prices. But the biggest stressor for her right now is finding and keeping staff, a situation that's also rooted in affordability. Owens has another coffee spot across the river in Warsaw. She's been short-staffed between both locations for months at a time. Rents have increased in this rural area, where the median income is around $50,000 a year. She says she's had to help employees find places to live and she's even put them up temporarily in a motel. Transportation is another problem: some workers don't have cars or are squeezed too much by current gas prices. "We have about five employees right now that we carpool to work," she says.   
   All of this means Owens has had to take shifts in the kitchen, putting off her front-of-house duties and paperwork to her evenings and days off. She says it's the same with other local restaurant owners: they're working themselves to the bone.   Owens won't discuss midterm politics, even though what she's learned about the lack of housing and transportation in the area has prompted her to run for the non-partisan town council. Tappahannock is in the eastern part of Virginia's 1st Congressional District, where the race between long-time Republican incumbent Rob Wittman and Democrat Shannon Taylor, the commonwealth's attorney for Henrico County, has been tight. Owens says whoever wins, she wants them to understand what small businesses like hers are dealing with these days. "We're struggling," she says, bluntly.   Jameka Campbell, who works across the river in Richmond County, thinks politicians are out of touch with the today's economic reality.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jameka Campbell, office manager at the Menokin historical site in Richmond County, Virginia, stands in the rebuilt section of the home of Francis Lightfoot Lee. It will be left partially restored to better showcase 18th century architecture and design.
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   "I think they need to get like Cardi B and go back to the grocery store and actually shop. ... see what those prices really look like, versus having someone else go out and purchase for them," she says.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jay Richardson Grebe, executive director of Just Harvest Va, collects ripe tomatoes from the organization's garden at Menokin
                
                    Melissa Gray/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray/NPR
    

   
   Campbell is raising two children and working two jobs at Menokin, a historical site originally owned by Francis Lightfoot Lee, a signer of the Declaration of Independence and a slave owner. She's an office manager there, as well as the community and outreach director with the nonprofit Just Harvest Va, which maintains gardens at Menokin. The goal is food sovereignty, Campbell explains, helping BIPOC communities with education and training around growing fresh food. "We make a way for you to be able to provide," she says, "so farm to table, we give you the instructions on how to cultivate your own land, how to cultivate the land around you."    Campbell says she has learned a lot about the economy of growing and cooking your own food from her grandmothers. She's also got a not-so-secret superpower: she's mastered the coupon deals at Walgreens.   
   "It's very neat. It's organized. The people are friendly," she says of her favorite one, in Callao a few miles away from Menokin. "My goal is always to only come in here once a month and spend $100," for household supplies, she says. She uses the Walgreens app to clip, save and track. She watches the sales and when there's a good deal, she'll stock up.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jameka Campbell compares sale prices on laundry scent boosters at Walgreens. She's not a big fan of the one that smells like leather.
                
                    Melissa Gray
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray
    

   
   Take her favorite laundry detergent: $4.99 for a small 27.5 ounce jug, perfect for her high-efficiency washing machine. "It's usually 'buy one, get two free,'" she says. So she'll triple her buying power when it's on special and buy in bulk. Also, she says, "you can earn $4 Walgreens cash rewards when you buy four more select items" like Secret deodorant or Gillette shaving cream and razors. She's also strategic at the register, checking out in batches so she can apply rewards from one transaction to the next. She makes sure to spend the rewards the same day.   On a recent trip, she got two 12-pack rolls of toilet paper, facial tissues, Lysol, dish detergent, disinfectant wipes, some laundry detergent pods, two boxes of disposable bathroom cups, three laundry scent boosters, toothpaste, a toothbrush and mouthwash. She spent $60.04 cents and saved $27.71.   Enough for a meal or "a quarter tank of gas," Campbell says.   In addition to her personal budget, Campbell says she's keeping her eyes on the candidates this midterm election and doing her research. "I'm going to look at what they've done in the past," she says, "then also do a deep dive on essentially, like, 'What properties do you own? What does that look like? Where do you live at, for real? Do you have, like, the house in the Hamptons, or are you living rurally?'"   And if the people in her district are not actually representing her the way she thinks they should, "then they have to go," she says. She'll make a decision on who to vote for closer to election day.   
   For right now, Campbell says she's doing ok. "I'm not rich. I'm not poor. I'm in between. And you know, it could go either way," she adds. "On any day, I could hit the lottery and be the richest person in the county I live in. I could lose both jobs in an instant and be the poorest person in the county that I live in."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                An art installation and a recreated slave dwelling at the Menokin historical site, in Richmond County, Virginia
                
                    Melissa Gray
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Melissa Gray
    

   
   Throughout Menokin there are reminders of the enslaved in art installations, historical artifacts and a recreation of a slave dwelling. Sometimes, when Campbell feels the strain of high prices, she thinks about the enslaved people who once farmed Menokin. "If they went through all of that," she says, "I think 'I can do this.' And I go do it."

schema.headline: Living with high prices in Virginia's 1st Congressional District

title: What NPR's senior political correspondent is watching for on Election Night
description: An NPR senior political editor/correspondent tells us what he will be looking out for as results roll in on Election Day.
body:
An NPR senior political editor/correspondent tells us what he will be looking out for as results roll in on Election Day.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  As the old cliche goes, the only poll that matters is the one on Election Day. Domenico Montanaro is NPR's senior political editor and correspondent, and he joins us now to talk about what he'll be watching for as the results roll in on Tuesday. Hi there, Domenico.DOMENICO MONTANARO, BYLINE: Great to be with you. Let's go.RASCOE: Let's go.MONTANARO: (Laughter).RASCOE: As polls start to close on Tuesday, what will you be looking for in the early results?MONTANARO: Yeah. I mean, one of the big things I'm watching on election night is Republican turnout. If Republicans have a high level of turnout on election night, that could really mitigate some of these Democratic gains that are expected. If they have a low turnout, then we could see a real washout across the country.So early on, we're going to start to see results come in in the 6 p.m. Eastern time hour. And two races I'm particularly watching are the 5th Congressional District in Indiana and the 6th Congressional District in Kentucky because Kentucky is a close race. And we're not sure which way it's going to be going, and we're going to see what those margins are. In Indiana 5 - that's incumbent Victoria Spartz's district - she's expected to win. But if she's in a tighter race than expected, look out for the rest of the night and for what that could mean for the House.Also, in Florida - Florida, also, we're going to see a lot of results start to come in fairly early on. And, you know, look at a place like Florida 22. That is a huge Latino population. If you're seeing Democrats do well in a place like that, that could mean a big sweep across South Florida and South Texas for what we see later on.RASCOE: We'll have a lot of races closing at 9 p.m. Eastern time. How will your focus have shifted by that time?MONTANARO: From a trickle to a fire hose. I mean, at 9 p.m., we're looking at Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. All will have results coming in. And we're going to really have a good sense, especially in the House, 'cause it's only a three-seat majority for Republicans. We're going to start to get a real sense of whether or not Democrats take over the House in the 9 p.m. hour.RASCOE: Talk to me about the Senate. There's lots of news about lots of races. The president is in Iowa and Kansas today. Alaska is competitive. Will we have to wait until the last polls close there, well past midnight Eastern time, to know which party controls the Senate?MONTANARO: God, you are giving me my worst-nightmare scenario...RASCOE: OK.MONTANARO: ...Which is quite possible because Alaska is one of those places that is looking really close right now - a toss-up state, a red state that Trump won but looks very, very close, and it counts votes very, very slowly. It has rank-choice voting. They didn't decide their races sometimes till three weeks later. If we're stuck in a mess of three weeks waiting to know control of the Senate, there's going to be a whole heck of a lot of misinformation going on. We know that President Trump's already laying the groundwork to say that the election was rigged. You know, it's better to have decisive victories one way or the other in this country because close elections tend to now be contested.But look. You've got five toss-up seats that are in red states, all places Trump won by double digits in the 2024 presidential election. And again, here's where Republican turnout is really going to matter. If Trump can get that base out, you know, you could be looking at a one- or two-seat Democratic net pickup in the Senate. And remember, they need four seats to take control of the Senate. If Republican turnout's not great, you know, you could be looking at six or seven seats that go toward Democrats.RASCOE: When you watch the exit polls come in, what will you be looking for in what people are saying they care about?MONTANARO: Yeah. There's a couple of numbers that I'm looking for. No. 1, when it comes to 18- to 29-year-olds, you know, they turn out at a very low percentage in midterm elections. They have - they see the steepest drop-off from presidential elections of any subgroup. And I'm looking to see if Democrats can win young voters by more than 20 points. I think that margin is going to be really key.I'm also looking for how Latinos wind up voting in, again, South Florida and South Texas. Remember, Trump won 46% of them in the 2024 presidential election, the highest ever for a Republican presidential candidate. They have been really soured on Trump, according to polls - 27% approval rating, for example, in the latest NBC Telemundo poll. And finally, the third thing I would look for is the number 46% when it comes to how Republicans do with independents. In the Trump era, when Republicans have gotten 46% or more with independents, they've seen success. When they've been below that, in two elections, they have not - 2018 and 2020.RASCOE: That's NPR's Domenico Montanaro. Domenico, thanks so much.MONTANARO: You're so welcome. Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: Politics chat: Data centers are on everyone's minds going into Election Day
description: With days until Election Day, polls show momentum for Democratic candidates and bipartisan distaste for data centers.
body:
With days until Election Day, polls show momentum for Democratic candidates and bipartisan distaste for data centers.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  Heading into this last weekend before Election Day, nearly 50 million people have already voted, either in person or by mail. The total vote in 2022's midterms was 112 million. This year's on pace to beat that number. NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson joins us now. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: So where do things stand this morning from your point of view?LIASSON: Well, Republicans and Democrats agree privately that the House will most likely go to the Democrats. It's unclear about the margin, probably a bigger one than the tiny majority that Republicans have now. Both sides say they are optimistic about the Senate. Of course, someone has to be wrong. Either Democrats will win the Senate majority, or Republicans will hold onto it.The handful of races that are going to determine the majority in the Senate are all still polling within the margin of error. That means that they're too close to call. Democrats will probably pick up seats in the Senate, but it's not clear if they will get the net four pickups they need to take control. And the states that are going to determine that are Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, a lot of red states.RASCOE: Campaigns are making their final arguments, and, you know, those are going to vary race to race. In general, though, are there any issues that have risen to the top of voters' minds that stands out to you?LIASSON: Yes, data centers. That was surprising. In the beginning of the cycle, it wasn't clear they would be such a big issue. States had been competing to get data centers to come to their states, but it turns out they are very unpopular. That sentiment is bipartisan. It's an example of the kind of economic populism that we see converging from the left and right. It's why you saw Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon appear at the same anti-AI conference.And data centers is the way that AI is most present to voters in their own communities. Majorities don't want them there. And it's caused some pretty dramatic flip-flops. Incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott courted data centers for years. All of a sudden, now he's for a moratorium.And I think they've become a proxy for the backlash against billionaires. You know, the rich get richer while you can't afford gas. And the debate over the data centers also illustrates another big theme of the campaign, which is that Donald Trump is on the opposite side of majority popular opinion. On issue after issue, this is true - on Iran, on tariffs. On data centers, he says he's for them. He's called them a golden goose for the economy. He was in Ohio in October at a rally with Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted. He said, we want data centers. He says, you can't turn them off. They'll go to China.RASCOE: October has come and gone. Were there any so-called October surprises?LIASSON: Well, I would say the closest thing to an October surprise is the double Dan Sullivan situation in Alaska. The Republican governor there says he's starting an investigation. President Trump has asked his Department of Justice to investigate how Daniel J. Sullivan got on the ballot. The incumbent senator is Dan S. Sullivan. There was some reporting in The New York Times that the Mary Peltola campaign - she's the Democratic candidate - was deeply involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola denies that. The big question is, is any of this illegal?RASCOE: I mean, that is a big question. Alaska's Supreme Court ruled in June that both Sullivans could appear on the ballot. And this is far from the first example of political parties, for lack of a better term, gaming the vote.LIASSON: That's right. It happens a lot. Both parties do it. There are some examples this cycle. And one of them in Ohio, a Republican group, spent more than $2 million to promote a socialist candidate in the Senate race named Greg Levy. They're hoping to pull away votes from the Democratic candidate, former Senator Sherrod Brown.So sometimes it's a person with a similar name, like in Alaska. Sometimes it's a person who's on the extreme of the opposite party, and the other party backs them in an effort to try to split the vote. Remember when Trump's allies tried to get Kanye West to run for president in hopes that he could split the Black vote? It's just unclear what, if any, laws these kinds of political shenanigans would break.RASCOE: And yet the Justice Department is moving forward with its lawsuit about this, right?LIASSON: That's right. They're asking a judge to separate all ballots in Alaska showing votes for the second Dan Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan, until it can be determined if voters really meant to vote for him. Alaska officials say that would be impossible.The Trump administration has also filed a lawsuit to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race in case the Republican loses, but Trump doesn't have a good track record in court on these kinds of suits. Last week, U.S. judge Trina Thompson ordered the administration to stop threatening state and local election officials with prosecution if they didn't refuse to issue ballots to people the administration says may be ineligible to vote. So this all adds up to what Trump's critics argue is an effort to try to take control of elections, overturn the results if they don't go his way.RASCOE: That's NPR's Mara Liasson. Mara, thank you so much.LIASSON: You're welcome.
